what: Ultrapar is a Brazilian group built around fuel distribution. Its main business, Ipiranga, supplies and franchises thousands of petrol stations across Brazil. It also owns Ultragaz, which distributes bottled cooking gas, and Ultracargo, which operates liquid bulk storage terminals at Brazilian ports.
customers: Brazilian motorists through franchised Ipiranga stations, households and small businesses buying bottled gas from Ultragaz, and fuel and chemical companies renting tank storage at Ultracargo’s port terminals.
money: Wholesale fuel supplied to franchised and company-operated service stations.
Liquefied petroleum gas in cylinders and bulk, mainly for cooking.
Liquid bulk terminals at Brazilian ports, the highest-margin business.
moat: Fuel distribution in Brazil is a scale and logistics business: thousands of stations, a distribution network and a recognised brand that franchisees want above the door. Ultracargo is better still — port terminal capacity is permitted, physical and effectively impossible to replicate, which is why it earns far higher margins than the fuel it stores.
risks: Net margin of 1.7% on $27.3B of revenue is the reality of fuel distribution: enormous turnover, almost no margin, and no protection if volumes fall.
Brazilian fuel distribution has a persistent problem with tax evasion and irregular competitors, which undercuts compliant distributors on price.
Revenue has swung widely with fuel prices, from $19.7B to $27.2B to $21.6B, so the headline figure says little about the business.
The share price is in dollars while the earnings are in reais, so a currency move alone can change the return for a foreign holder.
Government intervention in Brazilian fuel pricing has a long history and is outside any company’s control.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 5.5 times earnings, 4.1 times EV/EBITDA and 0.21 times sales — very low multiples even allowing for the business mix.
Free cash flow of $1.1B against a $5.8B market value is a 19% yield.
Ultracargo’s port terminals are an infrastructure asset with high margins and almost no competitive threat, and it is worth far more than its share of revenue suggests.
Bottled cooking gas demand is a staple in Brazil, which makes Ultragaz steady regardless of economic conditions.
Eight analysts average a $7.18 target, about 38% above the current price.
watch: Fuel distribution volumes and margin per litre, separately from revenue. Revenue moves with fuel prices and tells you nothing; litres sold and the cents earned on each one tell you everything.
view: The first thing to do with Ultrapar is ignore the revenue line entirely. Twenty-seven billion dollars of revenue sounds like a large company; a 1.7% net margin tells you that almost all of it is the cost of the fuel passing through. Revenue here moves with the oil price and the real, not with the business. The only numbers that describe fuel distribution are litres sold and the margin per litre, and anyone tracking this company on anything else is watching the weather.

Within the group there are really two different businesses wearing one share price. Ipiranga is a vast, thin-margin logistics operation — thousands of stations, a recognised brand, scale economics, and a persistent competitive problem from distributors who evade fuel taxes and therefore undercut the compliant ones. It is a decent business in a difficult industry. Ultracargo is something else entirely: permitted liquid bulk terminals at Brazilian ports, physically impossible to replicate, earning high margins on infrastructure that nobody can build alongside. It is a small share of revenue and a large share of what the company is actually worth.

At 5.5 times earnings, 4.1 times EV/EBITDA and a 19% free cash flow yield, the market is pricing the whole thing as though it were only the thin-margin fuel distributor, in a country investors have repeatedly decided they do not want to own. Some of that discount is deserved. Brazilian governments have intervened in fuel pricing before and will again, and a dollar investor carries currency risk that can wipe out an operating year’s progress on its own.

My view is that this is genuinely cheap rather than apparently cheap, and that the terminals are the reason. But it is cheap for reasons that are unlikely to disappear — Brazil risk, currency, fuel tax evasion, political intervention — so the return has to come from cash flow and dividends rather than from a re-rating. That is an acceptable way to make money provided you understand that is the deal, and provided you watch volumes and margin per litre rather than the headline figures.
bull: Fuel volumes and margin per litre hold while Ultracargo’s irreplaceable port terminals compound, and a 19% free cash flow yield pays the holder regardless of re-rating.
bear: Tax-evading competitors keep taking share at 1.7% margins, Brazilian fuel policy intervenes again, and currency erodes a dollar investor’s return.
